# Varish Partners: full site content
Source: https://www.varishpartners.com/

> Varish Partners is a tax, finance and strategic advisory firm in Mangaluru, India, serving founders, promoters, startups and established businesses. The firm combines direct and indirect tax, CFO-level financial advice, strategy, transactions and cross-border work, led by its partners rather than delegated.

- Business Setup, Compliance & Governance: Building the financial and regulatory foundation for businesses.

## Meet Our Leadership

Meet our dedicated professionals, committed to providing top-notch financial consultancy, tax compliance, and business advisory services tailored to your needs.

### Varun Shenoy

Managing Partner

vshenoy@varishpartners.com
Varun is a consultant and CA Final candidate specialising in strategy and business advisory, with expertise spanning growth and expansion, finance and taxation, capital raising and structuring, economic and corporate laws, capital markets, and entrepreneurship.

An entrepreneur himself, Varun co-founded Health-E, a health-tech platform, in 2020. This experience shaped his understanding of the challenges involved in building and scaling businesses, from strategy and finance to execution.

His perspectives on entrepreneurship, economics, taxation, corporate laws and finance have been featured at platforms including the i5 Summit at IIM Indore, Anveeksha at AIMIT, and national conferences organised by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI).

Over the course of his professional journey, Varun has worked with businesses across technology, e-commerce, real estate, construction, consumer goods and retail, as well as listed companies. His engagements have included strategic expansion, cross border transaction advisory, capital raising and financial structuring, due diligence, providing exposure to businesses at different stages of growth and across diverse sectors.

At Varish Partners, Varun leads client relationships and contributes to business strategy, finance and the firm’s overall management. He works closely with founders, promoters and management teams on strategic decisions, growth initiatives, capital requirements and complex financial matters.

# Our Story
Source: https://www.varishpartners.com/our-story/

Varish Partners was built on a simple observation: most businesses don't fail their financial and tax obligations out of neglect — they fail them because good advice arrives too late, or too generic to act on. Founded by Varun Shenoy and Vishwanath Prabhu, professionals with over two decades of combined experience across tax, compliance, and corporate advisory, the firm set out to close that gap: advice that arrives before a decision is made, not after it's already cost something.

What started as tax and compliance support for individuals and small businesses grew, as our clients grew, into a full consultancy practice — covering business registration, GST, financial planning, fractional CFO support, and transaction advisory. The common thread has stayed the same throughout: we work alongside clients through the year, not just at deadlines, and we measure our work by whether it actually moved the client's business forward.

### A Story That Defines How We Work

One engagement in particular captures what that looks like in practice. A client came to us for their overseas expansion — advice on the right investment strategy, and a way through the complexity of cross-border taxation and transfer pricing. The timelines were tight, so the team built a comprehensive proposal upfront, laying out exactly where we'd focus and why, then worked through the engagement with the same discipline: a concise final report, risks clearly categorised, delivered on schedule.

The result was concrete — the client moved into a new international market with an anticipated 20% increase in investment potential, and the risk mitigation work built into our advice is expected to cut their compliance costs by roughly 25%. It's one of many client stories, but it's a fair example of the standard we hold ourselves to: proactive planning, clear deliverables, and outcomes clients can actually measure.

### Where we are today

Today, Varish Partners supports individuals, startups, and established businesses across tax consultancy, GST compliance, financial planning, and business advisory — the same client-first approach the firm was founded on, applied at a larger scale. Read more about our mission, values, and leadership, or get in touch to start a conversation.

---

# Tax Advisory & Compliance
Source: https://www.varishpartners.com/tax-consultancy-compliances/

Helping businesses manage tax efficiently, compliantly and strategically.

Tax touches almost every decision a business makes, from how it is structured to how it prices, pays and grows. We advise on direct and indirect tax together, so the position you take in one never creates a problem in the other, and we stay with you through filings, reviews and disputes.

What all includes

## Direct & Indirect Tax Advisory

Income tax and GST are usually handled by different people, which is where gaps and double costs appear. We look at both together, advise on the tax impact of day-to-day business decisions, and give you clear positions you can rely on when filing and when questioned.

## Corporate & International Tax

Companies face questions on residence, permanent establishment, foreign income and cross-border payments as soon as they deal overseas. We advise on corporate tax positions at home and on how international activity is taxed, so profits are not taxed twice and reporting stays consistent.

## Tax Planning & Structuring

The right structure, set up early, saves far more than any year-end adjustment. We review how your business, its entities and its owners are organised and recommend arrangements that are efficient, commercially sensible and able to stand up to scrutiny.

## Transaction Tax Advisory

Acquisitions, share sales, mergers and restructurings each carry tax consequences that can change the value of the deal. We model those consequences before terms are fixed and advise on structures that protect value for buyers, sellers and promoters.

## GST Advisory & Compliance

We handle GST registrations, monthly and annual returns, reconciliations and input tax credit reviews, and advise on classification, place of supply and e-invoicing questions. The aim is simple: no credit lost to avoidable errors and no surprises when the department asks questions.

## TDS & Withholding Tax Advisory

Getting withholding wrong leads to interest, disallowed expenses and unhappy vendors and employees. We advise on the correct rates and sections for domestic and foreign payments, manage quarterly returns and certificates, and help with lower-deduction applications where they apply.

## Tax Reviews & Health Checks

A periodic review finds exposures while they are still cheap to fix. We go through your income tax, GST and TDS positions, filings and records, and give you a clear list of gaps, their likely cost and the steps to close them before an audit or notice does it for you.

## Transfer Pricing Advisory

Transactions between related entities must be priced as if they were between strangers. We help set and document arm’s length pricing for goods, services, royalties and funding, prepare the required reports, and support you when those prices are examined.

## Tax Due Diligence

Before you invest in or buy a business, you need to know what tax history comes with it. We review past filings, open assessments and risky positions, quantify the exposure, and suggest how it should be handled in the price, warranties or indemnities.

## Tax Litigation & Representation

When a notice, assessment or demand arrives, the quality of the first response often decides the outcome. We draft replies, represent you before tax authorities and appellate forums, and manage disputes with a practical eye on both the merits and the cost of fighting.

Explore services
Schedule a call

Whether you need a single position reviewed or a long-term tax partner, we bring technical depth and practical judgment to every engagement. Contact us to discuss your tax position.

# CFO & Financial Advisory
Source: https://www.varishpartners.com/fractional-cfo-services/

Financial clarity and decision support for growing businesses.

Growing businesses need senior financial thinking long before they can justify a full-time CFO. We give founders and management teams clear numbers, honest analysis and a steady hand on cash, planning and reporting, so decisions are made on facts rather than instinct.

What all includes

## Fractional CFO Services

You get an experienced CFO for the days and hours your business actually needs. We lead the finance function, work alongside your team and advisers, and bring the discipline and perspective of a senior finance leader without the cost of a full-time hire.

## Board & Investor Reporting

Boards and investors want the same things: accurate numbers, a clear story and no surprises. We prepare board packs and investor updates that explain performance, flag risks early and show how the business is tracking against its plan.

## Business Performance Reviews

We step back and look at how the business is really doing across products, customers, locations and teams. The review shows where money is made and lost, how you compare with peers, and which few changes would make the biggest difference.

## Financial Planning & Analysis

Good planning turns strategy into numbers you can manage against. We build the planning cycle, analyse actual results against plan every month, and explain the variances in plain language so management knows what to do next.

## Budgeting & Forecasting

We prepare annual budgets that reflect how the business actually runs, and rolling forecasts that update as conditions change. You see where the year is heading early enough to act, not after the quarter has closed.

## Financial Modelling

A well-built model lets you test decisions before you commit to them. We build clear, auditable models for budgets, new projects, pricing, fundraising and expansion, with scenarios that show what happens when assumptions change.

## Cash Flow & Working Capital

Profitable businesses still fail when cash runs short. We forecast cash week by week, tighten collections, payables and inventory, and free up working capital so growth is funded from within wherever possible.

## Management Reporting & MIS

We design monthly MIS that management actually reads: the handful of numbers that matter, reported on time and in a consistent format. Dashboards and commentary make it easy to spot trends and act on them.

## Profitability & Cost Optimisation

We analyse margins by product, customer and channel to show which parts of the business earn their keep. Then we look at costs line by line and help you cut waste without damaging the things customers value.

## Financial Controls & Process Improvement

Weak processes lead to errors, delays and fraud. We review how money moves through the business, from purchase to payment and from sale to collection, and put in practical controls and cleaner processes that scale as you grow.

Explore services
Schedule a call

Whether you need a part-time CFO, a forecast you can trust or a clearer monthly picture, we will fit the support to the stage your business is at. Contact us to talk it through.

# Strategy & Growth Advisory
Source: https://www.varishpartners.com/strategic-consulting-impact/

Turning business ambitions into executable growth strategies.

Ambition is only useful when it becomes a plan people can act on. We help promoters and leadership teams decide where to compete, how to grow and how to fund that growth, including the government schemes and incentives that many businesses never claim.

What all includes

## Business & Corporate Strategy

We work with leadership to set a clear direction: which markets to play in, which businesses to grow or exit, and how resources should be allocated between them. The result is a strategy that is specific enough to guide everyday decisions.

## Business Model Design & Optimisation

How you make money matters as much as what you sell. We examine your revenue streams, cost structure and delivery model, and redesign them where needed so the business earns more from the same effort.

## Market & Competitive Analysis

We size your market, map the competitors and study what customers actually choose and why. This gives you a fact-based view of where the opportunities are and where you are exposed.

## Business Restructuring

When a business has outgrown its shape or is under pressure, restructuring can restore focus and viability. We plan and support changes to operations, entities, costs and finances, keeping stakeholders informed at every stage.

## Performance Improvement

We identify the few operational and financial levers that most affect results, set targets for them and track progress with management. The focus is on measurable improvement within months, not reports that sit on a shelf.

## Promoter & Management Advisory

Promoters carry decisions that no one else in the business can make for them. We act as a trusted sounding board on growth, succession, governance and personal wealth questions that sit alongside the business.

## Growth Strategy

We lay out the realistic paths to growth, whether new customers, new products, new geographies or acquisitions, and compare them on return, risk and what they demand from the organisation. You leave with a prioritised plan, not a wish list.

## Market Entry & Expansion Strategy

Entering a new city, state or country takes more than a good product. We assess demand, regulation, tax and competition in the target market and recommend the entry route, structure and timing most likely to succeed.

## Go-to-Market Strategy

We help you decide who to sell to first, through which channels, at what price and with what message. A clear go-to-market plan shortens the time from launch to steady revenue.

## Pricing & Revenue Strategy

Pricing is often the fastest route to better margins. We analyse your costs, customers and competitors and recommend pricing and discount structures that grow revenue without losing the customers who matter.

## Funding Requirement Assessment

Before raising money, you need to know how much, when and for what. We work out the real funding need from your plans and cash forecasts, so you raise enough to reach the next milestone without giving away more than necessary.

## Capital Structure Advisory

The mix of equity, debt and internal funds shapes your cost of capital, your control and your flexibility. We recommend a capital structure that suits your stage, cash flows and appetite for risk.

## Debt vs Equity Funding Strategy

Debt is cheaper but must be repaid; equity is patient but dilutes ownership. We compare the options available to you, including bank finance, NBFCs, venture debt and equity investors, and help you choose the right combination.

## Fundraising Readiness

Lenders and investors decide quickly, so your numbers, documents and story need to be ready before the first meeting. We prepare the financial model, information pack and data room, and help you answer the questions they will ask.

## Grant & Incentive Identification

Central and state governments offer grants, subsidies, tax benefits and concessional finance that many businesses never hear about. We review your business, sector and plans to identify the incentives you may be entitled to.

## Central & State Scheme Mapping

Schemes differ widely by state, sector and project size. We map the central and state schemes relevant to your investment, including industrial policies and production-linked incentives, so you can compare locations and plans on their full economics.

## Subsidy & Incentive Optimisation

The way a project is planned, located and phased can change how much support it qualifies for. We help you shape investments to maximise eligible benefits while keeping the commercial logic intact.

## Application & Documentation Support

Incentive applications are detailed and unforgiving of gaps. We prepare and file the applications, project reports and supporting documents, and follow up with the departments concerned until approval.

## Incentive Eligibility & Structuring

Eligibility often depends on the entity, its ownership, the investment category and the timing of spend. We structure your project and entity so it meets the conditions from the outset rather than discovering a mismatch later.

## Post-Sanction Compliance & Claim Support

Approval is only the start; benefits are paid out when conditions are met and claims are filed correctly. We track your obligations, prepare periodic claims and certifications, and help ensure the money you were promised actually arrives.

Explore services
Schedule a call

Whether you are planning your next phase of growth or looking for the funding and incentives to pay for it, we will help you build a plan you can execute. Contact us to start the conversation.

# Transaction & Corporate Advisory
Source: https://www.varishpartners.com/business-advisory-services/

Advising businesses through critical transactions and strategic events.

Acquisitions, sales, investments and restructurings are the moments that shape a business for years. We advise from the first idea to completion, bringing financial, tax and commercial judgment together so you negotiate from knowledge and close on terms that hold up.

What all includes

## M&A Advisory

We support buyers and sellers through the full deal process: identifying and approaching counterparties, evaluating the business, negotiating terms and managing the path to completion, so decisions are made with a clear view of value and risk.

## Acquisitions & Divestitures

Whether you are buying a business to grow or selling a part that no longer fits, we help you prepare, value, negotiate and complete the transaction, and plan the integration or separation that follows.

## Deal Structuring

The same price can be worth very different amounts depending on how a deal is structured. We advise on share versus asset deals, payment terms, earn-outs and consideration so the structure works commercially, legally and for tax.

## Joint Venture Advisory

A joint venture succeeds when the partners agree clearly on contributions, control and exit from the start. We help structure the venture, model its economics and set out the terms that keep the partnership workable.

## Strategic Investments

When you invest in another business, whether a minority stake or a strategic partnership, we assess the target, the fit with your own business and the terms on offer, so the investment supports your strategy rather than distracting from it.

## Financial & Tax Due Diligence

We examine the quality of earnings, working capital, debt and tax history of the business you are dealing with. Our findings feed directly into price, deal terms and protections, so there are fewer surprises after closing.

## Valuation & Financial Modelling

We value businesses and shares using methods that suit the purpose, whether a transaction, fundraising, regulatory filing or internal decision, and build models that show how value moves with each key assumption.

## Transaction Tax Advisory

Every transaction has tax consequences for both sides. We identify them early, compare alternative structures and advise on the approach that protects value while staying on solid technical ground.

## Corporate Restructuring

Group structures built up over years often become complex and inefficient. We advise on mergers, demergers, consolidations and simplifications that reduce cost and risk and make the group easier to manage and invest in.

## Shareholder & Promoter Advisory

We advise promoters and shareholders on ownership, shareholder agreements, family arrangements and the terms of new investment, helping protect their interests while keeping the business able to raise capital and grow.

## Succession & Business Transfer

Passing a business to the next generation, to management or to a buyer takes years of planning to do well. We help promoters plan the timing, structure and tax impact of the transfer so the business and the family are both protected.

Explore services
Schedule a call

Whether you are buying, selling, investing or reorganising, we will help you see the full picture before you commit. Contact us to discuss your transaction.

# Cross-Border & International Advisory
Source: https://www.varishpartners.com/cross-border-international-advisory/

Helping businesses navigate international expansion, investments and transactions.

Going international adds new layers of tax, foreign exchange rules and structuring choices. We advise Indian businesses expanding overseas and foreign businesses entering India, bringing international tax, FEMA and transaction experience together in one team.

What all includes

## Inbound Investment Advisory

Foreign investors coming into India need to know which sectors are open, which approval routes apply and how their investment will be taxed. We advise on the entry route, pricing and reporting requirements, and on how returns can be taken out efficiently.

## Outbound Investment Advisory

Indian businesses investing abroad must follow the overseas investment rules and plan for tax in both countries. We advise on the structure, funding and reporting of overseas investments so they stay compliant and tax-efficient.

## India Entry Strategy for Foreign Businesses

We help foreign companies choose how to enter India, whether through a subsidiary, branch, liaison office or partnership, and support them through setup, registrations and the first years of operation.

## International Expansion Planning

Before you expand into a new country, we help you compare markets on demand, regulation, tax and cost of operation, and plan a phased entry that limits risk while you learn the market.

## Overseas Subsidiary & Entity Structuring

The jurisdiction and form of your overseas entities affect tax, control and future flexibility. We design group structures that support your operations and funding plans and comply with the rules in every country involved.

## Cross-Border Transaction Advisory

Transactions that cross borders involve two tax systems, foreign exchange rules and often different accounting standards. We coordinate these moving parts so the deal is structured, priced and completed correctly on both sides.

## Cross-Border M&A Advisory

We advise on acquisitions and sales involving foreign buyers, sellers or targets, covering valuation, diligence, deal structure and the regulatory approvals and filings needed to close.

## Structuring of Intercompany Transactions

Services, royalties, loans and goods moving between group companies must be structured and priced carefully. We design intercompany arrangements and agreements that reflect real activity and hold up under tax review.

## Repatriation & Remittance Structuring

Getting profits and capital back from an investment should be planned from day one. We advise on the most efficient routes, whether dividends, interest, royalties, fees or buy-backs, and the tax and regulatory steps each one requires.

## Cross-Border Payment & Withholding Advisory

Payments to non-residents raise questions of withholding tax, treaty rates and remittance certification. We advise on the correct treatment before money leaves the country, so neither you nor the recipient faces demands later.

## International Tax Structuring

We design cross-border structures that are tax-efficient and have real commercial substance, taking into account treaties, anti-avoidance rules and global minimum tax developments that increasingly limit aggressive planning.

## Transfer Pricing

We help multinational groups set arm’s length prices for intercompany transactions, prepare benchmarking studies and documentation, and support audits and disputes in India and abroad.

## Double Taxation & Treaty Advisory

Tax treaties can reduce or remove double tax, but only if their conditions are met and properly documented. We advise on treaty eligibility, residency certificates and foreign tax credits so income is not taxed twice.

## FEMA & Regulatory Advisory

Foreign exchange rules govern how money and investments move in and out of India. We advise on FEMA and RBI requirements, handle the required filings, and help resolve delays or defaults through compounding where needed.

Explore services
Schedule a call

Whether you are taking your business abroad or bringing your business to India, we will help you do it with the right structure from the start. Contact us to discuss your plans.

# Startup & Venture Advisory
Source: https://www.varishpartners.com/start-up-advisory-and-consultancy-services/

From incorporation to institutional capital and scale.

Founders have to get a lot right early, often with little time and less money. We help startups set up properly, raise capital on sensible terms and build the finance function investors expect, so the business is ready for each stage before it arrives.

What all includes

## Startup Structuring

The entity you choose and how ownership is set up on day one affect fundraising, taxes and exits years later. We help founders choose the right structure, including where international founders or investors are involved, and set it up cleanly.

## Founder & Promoter Advisory

We act as a sounding board for founders on equity splits, vesting, founder agreements, personal tax and the financial side of big decisions, so the relationships at the top stay clear as the company grows.

## Business Planning

We turn your idea into a plan with clear milestones, costs and revenue assumptions. A realistic plan keeps the team aligned and gives investors confidence that you understand your own business.

## Startup Tax Advisory

Startups face specific tax questions around share issues, investor funding, ESOPs and eligible tax holidays. We advise on these early so tax does not become an obstacle during a funding round or due diligence.

## Government Startup Schemes & Incentives

Recognition under the Startup India programme and various state policies can bring tax benefits, grants and easier compliance. We check your eligibility, handle the applications and help you use the benefits available.

## Fundraising Strategy

We help you decide how much to raise, when, from whom and on what instrument, whether equity, convertible notes or venture debt, so each round moves the company forward without unnecessary dilution.

## Investor Readiness

We get your numbers, documents and pitch ready before you meet investors: clean financials, a credible model and a data room that answers questions before they are asked.

## Financial Modelling

We build startup models that investors can follow, linking growth drivers, unit economics, hiring and burn to show how the business reaches its milestones and what happens if assumptions slip.

## Cap Table Structuring

A cap table that is messy or poorly planned can scare off investors. We keep your cap table accurate, model dilution across future rounds and advise on investor rights and share classes.

## ESOP Advisory

Stock options help startups attract and keep good people. We design ESOP schemes, advise on the size of the pool, vesting and valuation, and explain the tax treatment clearly to the company and employees.

## Due Diligence Readiness

We review your records, filings and contracts the way an investor would and fix the gaps before diligence begins, so the round is not delayed or repriced over issues you could have solved in advance.

## Virtual CFO / CFO Support

As you scale, you need senior finance support long before you can hire a full-time CFO. We run your finance function part-time, covering reporting, cash, compliance and investor relations.

## Investor Reporting

Regular, honest investor updates build trust for the next round. We prepare monthly and quarterly reports and board materials that show performance, cash position and progress against plan.

## Exit & Liquidity Planning

Whether the goal is an acquisition, a secondary sale or a public listing, we help founders and investors plan the exit, understand its tax impact and prepare the company to achieve the best value.

Explore services
Schedule a call

Whether you are about to incorporate or preparing for your next round, we will help you build the financial foundations investors look for. Contact us to talk to our team.

# Risk & Due Diligence
Source: https://www.varishpartners.com/risk-due-diligence/

Independent insight into financial, tax and business risks.

Good decisions depend on knowing what could go wrong. We give investors, buyers, lenders and management an independent view of the financial, tax and business risks in front of them, clearly explained and quantified wherever possible.

What all includes

## Financial Due Diligence

We test the numbers behind a business: the quality and sustainability of earnings, working capital, debt and off-balance-sheet items. You learn what you are really paying for and where the price or terms should change.

## Tax Due Diligence

We review past income tax, TDS and related filings, open assessments and aggressive positions, and estimate the potential exposure, so it can be addressed through price, indemnities or pre-closing fixes.

## GST Due Diligence

GST exposures can build up quietly through wrong classifications, credit claims or missed reconciliations. We examine returns, credits and notices to identify liabilities before they become yours.

## Business & Commercial Due Diligence

We look at the market, customers, competitors and business model to test whether the growth story holds up. This helps you judge whether the plan you are backing is realistic.

## Pre-Investment Due Diligence

Before you invest in a company, whether a startup or an established business, we give you a focused review of its finances, compliance and key risks, scaled to the size of the investment and the time available.

## Transaction Due Diligence

For acquisitions, mergers and sales, we coordinate financial, tax and commercial diligence into one clear report, highlighting the issues that affect value and the protections you should seek in the agreement.

## Risk Assessment

We help management identify and rank the risks facing the business, from financial and tax to operational and regulatory, and agree practical actions and owners for the ones that matter most.

## Internal Control Reviews

We test whether your internal controls work in practice, not just on paper, and recommend improvements that reduce errors and fraud without slowing the business down.

Explore services
Schedule a call

Whether you are about to invest, buy, lend or simply want to know where your own business is exposed, we will give you an independent view you can act on. Contact us to discuss your requirements.

# Business Setup, Compliance & Governance
Source: https://www.varishpartners.com/business-registration-services/

Building the financial and regulatory foundation for businesses.

A business built on the right structure and clean compliance is easier to run, fund and sell. We help you set up correctly, keep your books and filings in order every month, and put in the controls and governance that growing businesses need.

What all includes

## Business Incorporation & Structuring

We help you choose between a private company, LLP, partnership or other form, and handle incorporation from name approval to the registrations needed to start trading.

## Entity & Ownership Structuring

How ownership is split between founders, family members, holding companies and investors affects control, tax and future deals. We design ownership structures that are simple today and flexible for tomorrow.

## GST Registration & Compliance

We handle GST registration in the right states and categories, file returns on time, reconcile input tax credit every month and respond to routine departmental queries.

## Accounting & Bookkeeping

We keep your books accurate and up to date, close the accounts every month and prepare financial statements you can rely on for decisions, lenders, investors and tax filings.

## Payroll & TDS

We run monthly payroll, compute tax deductions, manage provident fund and other statutory contributions, and file TDS returns and certificates on time, so employees are paid correctly and the business stays compliant.

## ROC & Corporate Compliance

We manage annual filings with the Registrar of Companies, board and shareholder meetings, statutory registers and event-based filings, so your company stays in good standing and avoids penalties.

## Regulatory Compliance

Beyond tax and company law, businesses must keep up with labour, shops and establishments, import-export and sector-specific rules. We track these obligations and handle the registrations and filings on your behalf.

## Compliance Health Checks

We review your tax, corporate and regulatory compliance in one exercise, identify gaps and penalties at risk, and give you a clear plan to put things right before an audit, fundraise or sale.

## Internal Controls

We put in place the approvals, checks and segregation of duties that protect the business from errors and fraud, sized to your team so controls help rather than slow down daily work.

## SOP & Process Development

Written procedures make work consistent and easier to delegate. We document your finance and compliance processes as clear standard operating procedures that new team members can follow from day one.

# India’s creator economy: a portfolio of revenue streams, not one tax category
Source: https://www.varishpartners.com/indias-creator-economy-revenue-streams-not-one-tax-category/

By Varun ShenoyManaging Partner · 9 October 2026 · 28 min read

Download the full paperPDF · 31 pages · 633 KB
Download

A finance lens for creators building a business. Research cut-off: 9 October 2026. General information, not individual tax advice.

Source note. Numbers in square brackets refer to the source register in Appendix A. Legal positions are separated from operating recommendations and illustrative calculations. Some statutory text was read through identified secondary reproductions; the register makes that distinction explicit. Market figures in sections 1 to 5 come from third-party research with different definitions; projections are labelled, and calculations marked as ours are illustrative.

## Executive summary

**The central argument:** India’s creator economy is large and widening, but income is thin and concentrated. It becomes durable when each revenue stream has a clear contract, tax position and record trail.

- **Scale is real.** Creators on influencer-marketing platforms grew from about 0.96 million in 2020 to 4.12 million in 2025, and two-thirds are now outside the big metros. Creator-influenced consumer spending is estimated at $350-400 billion a year. [17][19]

- **Income is thin.** Only 8-10% of creators monetise effectively, and most earn under ₹18,000 a month. The ISB-Hashfame data points to repeat paid work, not more followers, as the gap. [17][20]

- **Money is concentrated.** Brand sponsorships and ads were nearly 90% of creator monetisation in FY24, and each new avenue brings a different payer and a different tax treatment. [20][27]

- **Demand is moving to regional languages, smaller cities and longer brand relationships.** Brands want proof of audience quality and organised delivery. [17][20][22]

- **A creator is an operating business, not a tax category.** Platform payouts, campaigns, commissions, courses and merchandise need separate treatment.

- **GST follows aggregate turnover and the nature of the supply.** For a Karnataka service provider, the ordinary registration threshold is ₹20 lakh, including exports. Domestic promotional services generally attract 18%; not every creator product does.

- **Barter is not free.** A retained product can trigger benefit-related TDS. A product received in exchange for promotion can also be non-cash consideration for GST. These are separate tests.

- **Foreign payment does not automatically mean an export.** Check the contracting recipient, place of supply, permitted receipt and other statutory conditions before using zero-rating and an LUT.

- **Presumptive tax is an eligibility decision.** Creating content does not, by itself, make someone a specified professional. Commission income can also close the ordinary small-business route.

- **The compliance calendar changed in 2026.** Current income-tax references are to the Income-tax Act, 2025; the new RBI service-export EDF framework took effect on 1 October 2026.

## At a glance

**4.12 million**Creators on influencer-marketing platforms, 2025 [17][18]

**66%**Creators outside the eight big metros, 2025 [17][18]

**8-10%**Creators who monetise effectively [20]

**Nearly 90%**Of creator monetisation from advertising and brand sponsorships, FY24 [20]

**₹20 lakh**Ordinary GST registration threshold, services from Karnataka [1][2]

## 01India’s creator economy has outgrown the side-hustle label

The number of creators on India’s influencer-marketing platforms rose from about 0.96 million in 2020 to 4.12 million in 2025, roughly 33% a year. Creators outside the eight big metros are now two-thirds of the base. Audience grew with supply: average engagement rose from 1.8% to 7.2%, and annual creator campaigns grew from about 14,000 to 42,000 at about 3.6 times the average spend per campaign. [17][18]

The money around creators is larger than the money paid to them. BCG estimates that monetised creators (more than 1,000 followers) influence $350-400 billion of annual consumer spending, with a projection above $1 trillion by 2030. The ecosystem’s own direct revenue is much smaller: $20-25 billion today, with a projection of $100-125 billion by 2030. Treat the projections as projections. [19][20][21]

Counts differ because definitions differ. BCG’s 2-2.5 million is monetised creators; ISB’s 4.12 million is creators registered on influencer-marketing platforms; Kofluence puts active creators at 4.0-4.4 million. Use each as a range marker, not a census. [17][19][22]

Figure 1Creator base, 2020 and 2025

**20200.96 million · 44% outside the big metros**

**20254.12 million · 66% outside the big metros**

Source: ISB-Hashfame [17][18]. Bar lengths are in proportion to creator numbers.

Exhibit 1India’s creator economy in numbers

MeasureLatest figureSource

Creators on influencer-marketing platforms4.12 million in 2025, up from 0.96 million in 2020ISB-Hashfame [17][18]

Non-metro share of creators66% in 2025 (2.72 million), against 44% in 2020ISB-Hashfame [17][18]

Average engagement rate1.8% in 2020 to 7.2% in 2025ISB-Hashfame [17]

Monetised creators (1,000+ followers)2-2.5 millionBCG [19][20]

Consumer spend influenced by creators$350-400 billion a year; BCG projects more than $1 trillion by 2030BCG [19][20]

Direct creator-ecosystem revenue$20-25 billion today; BCG projects $100-125 billion by 2030BCG [20][21]

Influencer-marketing spend₹3,000-3,500 crore in 2025; estimated ₹4,500-5,000 crore by 2027Kofluence [22]

Digital advertising₹947 billion in 2025, up 26%, about 63% of total advertisingFICCI-EY [24]

Social media and online video ad spend₹21,057 crore and ₹20,004 crore respectivelydentsu-e4m [25]

YouTube’s creative ecosystemMore than ₹16,000 crore of GDP and 930,000 full-time-equivalent jobs, reported November 2025Oxford Economics for YouTube [26]

A comparison, with its limits: Kofluence’s ₹3,000-3,500 crore of influencer-marketing spend is roughly 3-5% of the digital advertising totals from FICCI-EY (₹94,700 crore) and dentsu-e4m (₹71,621 crore). The definitions differ, so read it as direction, not share. Creators influence far more spending than they directly collect. This is our calculation. [22][24][25]

**Implication**The market is real and widening. Treat the headline numbers as context for your own pricing and planning, not as a forecast of your income.

## 02Reach is broad, but income is thin and concentrated

The same studies that show growth also show how little of it reaches most creators. BCG reports that only 8-10% of India’s creators monetise effectively, and that the majority earn less than ₹18,000 a month. Kofluence’s 2024-25 survey finds only 12% of creators earn 75% or more of their income from social media; more than half earn under a quarter of it there. [20][23]

The ISB-Hashfame data explains part of the gap. Non-metro creators taking part in brand campaigns rose from about 38,000 to more than 408,000, yet most still do a single paid campaign a year. The ratio of campaigns to creators in that group fell from about 0.37 to about 0.10. The authors conclude that the next stage depends on repeat work, not on more entrants. [17][18]

Scale matters less than frequency. In ISB’s wage comparison, a nano creator completing two campaigns earns about 29% of the average rural salaried wage and about 20% of the urban one. Only a micro creator completing five campaigns approaches a full-time wage. Kofluence finds 61.1% of creators in the 1,000-10,000 follower tier. [17][22]

Surveys disagree on who counts. YouTube reports that for nearly two-thirds of creators earning on its platform, YouTube is their primary income. That is a population already earning on the platform, not all creators, which is why it sits beside Kofluence’s 12% rather than contradicting it. [23][26]

A rough sense of scale follows from two of the figures above. Divide Kofluence’s ₹3,000-3,500 crore of 2025 influencer-marketing spend by ISB’s 4.12 million creators and the average is about ₹7,300-8,500 per creator a year. This is our arithmetic across data sets with different definitions; it is not an income statistic. Its point is that the average is small and the distribution is uneven. [17][22]

Exhibit 2What the income evidence says

EvidenceFindingSource

Share monetising effectively8-10% of creators; most earn under ₹18,000 a monthBCG via BuzzInContent [20]

Dependence on social income12% earn 75% or more of income from social; over half earn under 25% thereKofluence [23]

Repeat brand workMost non-metro creators do one paid campaign a year; campaigns per creator fell from about 0.37 to about 0.10ISB-Hashfame [17][18]

Pay per short videoFrom about ₹500 per Instagram reel for nano creators to over ₹2 lakh for mega creatorsKofluence [23]

Income against wagesTwo campaigns for a nano creator is about 29% of a rural salaried wage; five for a micro creator approaches a full-time wageISB-Hashfame [17]

Platform viewNearly two-thirds of creators earning on YouTube say it is their primary incomeYouTube / Oxford Economics [26]

**Implication**Judge a business by repeat paying relationships and margin, not audience size. A creator with a few recurring payers and clean records is closer to a stable income than one with a bigger audience and a single campaign a year.

## 03Almost all the money comes from two sources, and each new source brings its own paperwork

BCG found that advertising and brand sponsorships made up nearly 90% of creator monetisation in FY24. Kofluence’s survey is consistent: 47% of creators depend on sponsored collaborations and only 15% earn mainly from platform ad revenue. The dependence is a commercial risk. It is also a finance risk, because one kind of payer is easy to track and several are not. [20][23]

The other avenues are real but uneven. Platform programmes have thresholds. YouTube lists 1,000 subscribers plus either 4,000 qualified watch hours or 10 million qualified Shorts views in 90 days for ad revenue, and a lower 500-subscriber tier for memberships, with availability that depends on the country. The 4,000 hours are qualified long-form watch hours over the last 365 days. The 500-subscriber tier also needs 3 public uploads in the last 90 days, plus either 3,000 qualified long-form watch hours in the last 365 days or 3 million qualified Shorts views in the last 90 days. BCG describes virtual gifting as microtransactions of ₹10-100 on regional platforms, subscriptions as held back by price sensitivity, and live commerce as still early in India. [20][27]

The less visible point is that every avenue has a different payer, a different place of supply and a different tax treatment. Adding revenue streams is therefore also adding compliance work. Exhibit 3 maps each avenue to the finance question it raises, with the section of this paper that covers it.

Exhibit 3Where creators earn, and what each avenue brings with it

AvenueWhat the evidence saysHow money arrivesFinance question (section)

Brand deals and sponsored contentNearly 90% of FY24 monetisation; 47% of creators depend on it [20][23]Fee per deliverable, sometimes plus a productGST rate (7), barter (8), TDS (10)

Platform ad revenue1,000 subscribers plus watch-hour or Shorts-view thresholds; 15% earn mainly here [23][27]Revenue share paid by the platform, often a foreign entityExport status (9), foreign withholding (12)

Fan funding on platformsMemberships, Super Chat, Super Thanks and Shopping have separate thresholds and country availability [27]Platform payouts in several categoriesStatement reconciliation (13)

Virtual gifts and live tipping₹10-100 microtransactions on regional platforms [20]Many small receipts through a platformRecords and reconciliation (13)

Affiliate and commerce linksNamed by BCG as a diversification route [20]Commission on salesCommission income and eligibility for presumptive tax (11); supply analysis (9)

Courses, digital products, merchandiseOwn-product revenue is a separate stream from content incomeDirect sales to buyersGST classification (7), stock and margin records (13)

Subscriptions and live commerceEarly in India; price sensitivity limits subscriptions, live commerce is still testing [20]Recurring fees or sales commissionRegistration threshold (7), records (13)

**Implication**Diversify on purpose. Before adding a revenue stream, decide who will pay, what you are supplying and how it will be recorded. Revenue you cannot reconcile is not yet income you can plan with.

## 04Demand is shifting to regional languages, smaller cities and longer relationships

The ISB-Hashfame study finds Hindi accounts for 42% of creators; regional languages together account for 58%. It identifies Bhojpuri and Kannada as markets where creator participation runs ahead of brand investment. Karnataka is one of the states that produces more creators than its share of population would predict. For a Karnataka creator working in Kannada, Tulu or Konkani, that is a positioning point worth testing against real campaign enquiries. [17][18]

Kofluence reports that more than 62% of creators have seen more regional and vernacular briefs from brands. Engagement in Tier III and IV markets was 4.5-5.5%, against 3-4% in metros, and campaign costs were significantly lower there. The second half of that sentence matters for pricing: a market with lower campaign costs can reward volume but punish thin margins. [22]

Brands say they want longer commitments. In Kofluence’s survey, 62% of brand professionals see better returns from long-term creator partnerships, and 13.3% link influencer marketing directly to revenue targets. BCG finds around 70% of surveyed brands plan to raise influencer budgets by 1.5-3 times over two to three years, while 74% name fake engagement as a concern. A creator who can show real audience quality and organised delivery has an advantage. [20][22]

Exhibit 4What brands are signalling, and how to respond

Brand signalEvidenceWhat it suggests for a creator

Budgets are growingAbout 70% of surveyed brands plan 1.5-3 times higher influencer budgets [20]Expect more briefs; screen for fit and payment terms

Preference for long relationships62% of brand professionals see better returns from long-term partnerships [22]Offer retainers and repeat packages, with clear scope

Accountability is rising13.3% link to revenue targets; 46.4% apply campaign-level performance accountability [22]Keep delivery and performance records ready for the brand

Authenticity concern74% of brands cite fake engagement [20]Audience quality can justify a higher price

Regional demandMore than 62% of creators saw more regional briefs [22]Language and local relevance are priced assets

Where the money sitsE-commerce is 23% of influencer-marketing spend and FMCG 19% [22]Know your category’s paying sectors and payment cycles

**Implication**Price for the relationship, not for a single post. A longer arrangement needs a contract that says what is delivered, what rights are licensed, whether GST is added and who bears the tax on any product.

## 05A serious creator business has a finance function before it has a team

Kofluence reports that 15.2% of India’s creators are now registered as business entities or GST-registered individuals. The same report points to ASCI disclosure norms, SEBI scrutiny and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act as pressures moving the industry towards formal compliance. The ISB-Hashfame authors make a related point: creators need access to the institutions available to other self-employed professionals and MSMEs. [18][22]

Most creator businesses grow in stages, and the finance work changes at each one. The stages below are our framework for planning, not a statutory classification. The thresholds that move a creator from one stage to the next are the subject of the rest of this paper: GST registration, withholding, export reporting and the choice of tax scheme.

Figure 2From side income to structured business
1. Side income2. Regular earner3. Registered professional4. Structured business

The stages are our framework for planning, not a statutory classification.

Exhibit 5Four stages of a creator business

StageTypical signalsFinance set-up that fits

1. Side incomeOccasional brand deals or first platform payoutsPAN and bank trail in order; keep every invoice, payout statement and TDS certificate

2. Regular earnerRepeat brand work, several platforms, products received as part of dealsA written revenue map; monthly tracking against the GST turnover threshold; written barter terms

3. Registered professionalGST registration, overseas platform income or foreign clientsExport file linking contract, invoice, bank receipt, LUT and EDF; reconciled TDS credits; a scheme decision backed by eligibility

4. Structured businessA team, own products, possibly more than one entityMonthly management accounts, contribution by revenue stream, entity and contract review, planned tax payments

The tax sections that follow are written for stages 2 to 4. A creator at stage 1 should still read them, because the records that matter later are cheapest to keep from the start.

**Implication**Know which stage you are in before the next deal, not after it. The cheapest time to set up records is before a threshold forces the question.

## 06The first task is to define the business, not to count followers

A channel is a distribution asset. It is not a complete description of the business earning the money. Two creators with similar audiences may have entirely different exposure: one supplies promotional content to Indian brands; another licenses content, earns overseas platform revenue and sells a physical product.

The useful unit of analysis is the revenue stream and its contract. Identify who owes the money, what is delivered, whether rights are licensed, and whether the creator acts on their own account or arranges someone else’s transaction. Those facts matter to export treatment, withholding and presumptive-tax eligibility. [3][5][6][8]

Exhibit 6A creator’s revenue map

StreamQuestion that changes the treatmentRecord to keep

Brand campaignsContent production, promotion, rights licensing, or a combination?Contract, scope, invoice, TDS certificate

YouTube / AdSenseWhich entity contracts and pays, and for what?Platform terms, payout statement, remittance proof

AffiliatesOwn-account service or commission / agency arrangement?Affiliate agreement and commission statement

Courses / digital productsWhat is supplied, to whom, and where?Product description, buyer location, sales records

MerchandiseOwn inventory or another seller’s commission model?Purchase and sales invoices, returns, stock records

Barter collaborationsWhat is promised in exchange, and is the product returned?Written barter terms, valuation, return evidence

The right advisory budget depends on the business’s complexity: the number of streams, entities, overseas arrangements and staff. A single annual price cannot describe every creator’s needs.

**Implication**Build a revenue map before choosing a return form, GST code or tax scheme. Follower count is not the decision rule.

## 07GST registration follows the whole business; the rate follows the supply

For a creator supplying services from Karnataka, the ordinary registration threshold is aggregate turnover above ₹20 lakh in a financial year. Aggregate turnover is computed across India for the same PAN and includes taxable supplies, exempt supplies, exports and inter-State supplies; GST itself is excluded. It is not the bank balance or profit. Lower service thresholds apply in certain states, and compulsory-registration provisions need separate review. [1][2]

Notification 10/2017-Integrated Tax gives threshold-based relief for inter-State taxable services. An overseas client alone therefore does not automatically compel a small service provider to register. Once registered, eligible exports may be made without payment of IGST under an LUT. The ₹40 lakh goods-only threshold is not a general threshold for a creator who also supplies services. [1][2][4]

Domestic advertising / promotional services generally sit in the 18% service-rate framework. The exact classification must follow the agreement. Merchandise, licensing, digital products and courses should not simply inherit the same code or rate. A creator-led course is not automatically exempt education. [9]

Exhibit 7Registration is a turnover test, not a domestic-sales test
₹12 lakh Indian campaigns + ₹7 lakh qualifying foreign platform services + ₹3 lakh own courses = **₹22 lakh aggregate turnover**

Illustration only: ₹12 lakh Indian campaigns + ₹7 lakh qualifying foreign platform services + ₹3 lakh own courses = ₹22 lakh aggregate turnover, before considering other supplies. The foreign stream is included even if it qualifies for zero-rating. This is our calculation, assuming all three are supplies of the same PAN. [1][2]

Contracts should say whether fees are exclusive or inclusive of GST. An all-in price can leave the creator funding the tax from the agreed fee. Separately recording GST also keeps it out of management revenue and profit.

**Implication**Track the registration threshold monthly across every channel. Price a campaign after classifying it, not after copying another creator’s invoice.

## 08A retained product can create tax exposure without creating cash

A phone, outfit or hotel stay may feel like a perk. In a commercial collaboration it can also be part of the business’s compensation. The absence of a bank transfer does not end the analysis.

CBDT Circular 12/2022 directly addresses social-media influencers. A product returned after use for the promotional service is not treated as a benefit / perquisite for that withholding rule; a retained product is. The circular survives the new Act to the extent consistent with it. Current benefit-related TDS is under section 393(1), Table 8(iv), commonly still called the old section 194R. [5][6][7]

The general rate is 10%, subject to the ₹20,000 annual benefit threshold and the payer conditions. The threshold concerns the provider’s aggregate benefits to the recipient, not each product separately. Where the benefit is wholly in kind, or the cash component cannot cover the tax, the provider must ensure the required tax is paid before releasing it. The creator and brand should agree the mechanics in advance. [5][6]

GST is a different test. If a product is consideration for a promised post, supply valuation must consider the non-money consideration; Rule 27 starts with open-market value. An unsolicited sample with no agreed promotional service is not automatically the same arrangement. Nor does the income-tax return-of-product rule settle whether a GST supply occurred. [10]

**Exhibit 8: The barter file**Keep the agreed deliverables; the product’s supported value; who retains ownership; whether and when it is returned; the invoice or valuation workings; and evidence of withholding or tax paid. Do not treat a brand’s TDS valuation as automatically the right GST value.

**Implication**Agree the tax and cash burden before accepting barter. A collaboration with no cash fee can still need cash to settle its tax obligations.

## 09Overseas platform income is an export only when the facts support it

The IGST Act’s export-of-services definition requires the supplier to be in India, the recipient outside India, the place of supply outside India, payment in convertible foreign exchange or RBI-permitted rupees, and the supplier and recipient not merely establishments of the same person. All conditions matter. [3]

Figure 3The five export-of-services conditions

- Supplier in India

- Recipient outside India

- Place of supply outside India

- Payment in convertible foreign exchange or RBI-permitted rupees

- Supplier and recipient not merely establishments of the same person

As described in the IGST Act’s export-of-services definition [3]. All conditions matter.

YouTube or AdSense income can qualify, but a platform label or a foreign bank credit is insufficient. Read the actual contracting entity and terms. Own-account services generally use the recipient-location rule under section 13(2), subject to the other place-of-supply provisions. Arranging or facilitating another person’s supply can raise the intermediary issue. [3]

CBIC Circular 230/24/2024 distinguishes an advertising agency providing services on its own account from an agent merely facilitating media supply. Indian viewers are not, merely by being viewers, the paying recipient in the circular’s fact pattern. This is useful reasoning, not a blanket ruling on every platform or affiliate agreement. [11]

A registered exporter using the without-payment route needs an eligible LUT and export invoices, return reporting and receipt evidence. LUT validity is for the financial year. The LUT does not fix a failed export condition, and zero-rated GST does not mean income-tax-free income. [3][4][14]

From 1 October 2026, RBI Regulation 3(2) requires an EDF for service exports within 30 days after the end of the invoice month. One EDF may cover that month’s exports to multiple recipients. For non-software services, the regulation also allows submission on or before receipt of payment; an Authorised Dealer can extend the filing period on a reasoned request. Ordinary creator promotional/content services should be assessed as non-software rather than assumed to be software merely because delivery is online. Confirm the filing route with the bank. [12]

The amended regulation generally requires service export proceeds to be realised and repatriated within nine months of the invoice, subject to applicable exceptions and extensions. This is distinct from GST receipt conditions. [12]

**Implication**Maintain one export file that connects contract, invoice, platform statement, bank receipt, LUT and EDF. A payout dashboard alone is not that file.

## 10TDS is an advance tax credit, not a universal rate for creators

Brands do not all buy the same service. A campaign may involve contractual production, professional services, royalty rights or a benefit in kind. The withholding analysis must match the transaction. The rate deducted does not by itself decide the creator’s final taxable profit or eligibility for a tax scheme. [5][8]

Exhibit 9Familiar labels and the current law

Familiar 1961 Act labelCurrent 2025 Act referenceGeneral rule, subject to payer and payment conditions

194C: contractual work393(1), Table 6(i)1% for an individual/HUF contractor; 2% for other contractors. ₹30,000 single-payment / ₹1 lakh aggregate thresholds.

194J: professional / technical fees, specified royalties393(1), Table 6(iii)Generally 10% for professional fees; 2% for specified technical-service / film-royalty cases. ₹50,000 threshold for relevant fee / royalty categories.

194R: benefits / perquisites393(1), Table 8(iv)10%; ₹20,000 annual benefit threshold. Retained-product guidance is especially relevant.

These are general resident-payee rules, not a recommendation to select the lowest rate. Advertising, production and rights arrangements need contract-level review. The table does not cover every payer, non-resident payment, PAN failure, certificate or other exception. [5][6]

Reconcile gross invoices, money received and TDS certificates. A ₹1 lakh fee with ₹10,000 withheld is generally not ₹90,000 revenue merely because ₹90,000 reaches the account. That is an illustration of the reconciliation, not a ruling that 10% is the correct rate for the campaign.

Creators hiring editors, agencies or consultants may also become deductors. Their entity type, turnover and payment category determine the obligation. Deduction by the brand does not discharge the creator’s own payer obligations. [5]

**Implication**Resolve the withholding category before the invoice is paid. Reconcile credits during the year, rather than discovering missing credits at return time.

## 11Presumptive tax depends on eligibility, not on being called a freelancer

The Income-tax Act, 2025 took effect on 1 April 2026. Tax year 2026-27 is under that Act; earlier-year returns remain under the old framework. Section 58 now contains the presumptive schemes often described by the old labels 44AD and 44ADA. [7]

The specified-profession route uses section 58(2), Table 3 and section 62(4). The normal gross-receipts limit is ₹50 lakh, rising to ₹75 lakh where cash receipts do not exceed 5%. Income is 50% of gross receipts or the higher profit claimed actually earned. Resident individuals and firms other than LLPs can qualify, subject to the conditions. [8]

Section 62(4) lists specified professions including legal, medical, engineering, architecture, accountancy, technical consultancy, interior decoration, information technology and company secretary, plus notified professions. Content creation is not a standalone listed profession. Using technology is not the same as practising information technology. A notified professional category may apply on the actual facts, but it should be documented, not assumed. [8]

For an eligible business, section 58(2), Table 1 provides the ₹2 crore limit, increased to ₹3 crore when cash receipts do not exceed 5%, with the 6% / 8% computation depending on qualifying receipt modes and timing, or higher profit claimed. The eligibility definition excludes specified professionals, commission / brokerage earners and agency businesses. Affiliate commission can therefore be a material obstacle, not a trivial label to rename. Companies and LLPs do not qualify for these routes. [8]

Presumptive income does not permit another deduction for every camera, trip or editor bill. Nor does it erase GST, export reporting or the need to prove receipts and eligibility. Compare it with actual books before electing it; lower-profit claims, audit rules and the business-route opt-out restrictions need separate review. [8]

**Implication**Obtain a reasoned eligibility position before choosing the scheme. A low-effort return is not a substitute for a defensible classification.

## 12Foreign withholding and Indian tax are two parts of the same income file

A resident and ordinarily resident individual is generally taxable in India on worldwide income. The rules differ for non-residents and residents who are not ordinarily resident. Receiving money from abroad does not by itself establish residence or the legal source of the income. [14]

Google says it collects US tax information from monetising YouTube creators and, where applicable, withholds tax on US-viewer earnings. With valid information, the applicable rate depends on residence, income category and treaty eligibility. Without valid information, the default withholding can extend further. Do not promise a universal India-US rate or assume every AdSense payment has the same US classification. [13]

Foreign tax credit is not automatic. Check the treaty and Indian rules, offer the corresponding income correctly, and retain the tax statement and proof of deduction or payment. Under the 2026 Rules, the department’s current guidance uses Form 44 and Rule 76, rather than telling creators to use legacy Form 67 for every year. The guidance specifies the filing timing and requires accountant verification for companies, or in other cases where foreign tax paid for the tax year is at least ₹1 lakh. [15]

The platform’s gross earnings, foreign withholding and net remittance should reconcile. The overseas deduction does not replace Indian return reporting, and foreign tax credit is not the same as a GST refund.

**Implication**Treat US tax information, Indian income reporting and foreign tax credit as a connected process. Review the relevant year’s form, not an old checklist.

## 13Durable income comes from records and margins, not from a bigger payout screenshot

Creators should know the contribution from each stream after production costs, platform or agency charges and the tax cash reserve. This is an operating recommendation, not a claim that every cost is deductible. A campaign with heavy rework can be less attractive than a smaller repeat contract. Under actual-profit taxation, ordinary expense deductibility depends on business purpose and statutory conditions. General revenue expenses must be incurred wholly and exclusively for the business or profession; personal and capital spending are not automatically deductible as current expenses. Cameras and computers may need capital-asset and depreciation treatment, and mixed-use costs need supported allocation. Income-tax deductions and GST input credit are separate analyses. [16]

Exhibit 10A monthly creator close

- Reconcile each platform statement and brand invoice to receipts, withholding, fees and outstanding balances.

- Update the PAN-wide turnover tracker and classify new products, contracts and barter arrangements.

- Keep expense evidence, asset records and the basis for business / personal allocations.

- Review GST reporting, export receipts, EDF status and the income-tax / advance-tax cash plan.

- Compare contribution by stream, unpaid work and customer concentration; keep personal withdrawals outside operating costs.

Presumptive taxation, where available, simplifies one part of tax computation. It does not answer whether a product line is profitable or whether the next campaign will fund payroll. [8]

**Implication**The goal is a small finance system that runs with the business. Annual filing should be its output, not the first time the numbers are assembled.

## What creators should ask

- Which stage of Exhibit 5 is my business in, and does my record-keeping match it?

- Which two or three payers account for most of my income, and what happens if one leaves?

- Do I have a written scope and rate for repeat work, not only a price per post?

- Can I explain what each payer is buying, and show the contract that supports that treatment?

- Does my GST turnover tracker include exports and non-cash commercial collaborations?

- Are my brand quotes clear on GST, rights, reimbursements, withholding and payment timing?

- If I call a receipt an export, can I prove all the conditions and connect it to the bank receipt?

- Who is tracking the new EDF requirement with my Authorised Dealer?

- If I use presumptive tax, what is the written eligibility basis, especially for commissions and mixed streams?

- Do the platform’s gross earnings, foreign tax and net payment reconcile to my Indian reporting?

- Which revenue stream leaves cash after production costs and the tax reserve?

## How Varish Partners helps

The starting point is a creator-business review: revenue streams, contracts, turnover, platform statements and the way cash moves. From that map, a tax and CFO advisory engagement can connect classification, GST, withholding reconciliation, export documentation, tax planning and monthly management reporting.

The scope should match the business. A creator taking their first paid campaign needs a different finance setup from a team selling courses, merchandise and overseas content rights. The objective is the same: clear treatment, reliable records and a view of what is actually earned.

If your business sits at stage 2 or 3 of Exhibit 5, a first review is most useful before a registration threshold, an export filing or a larger brand deal forces the question. Varish Partners is a tax and CFO advisory practice in Mangaluru, and the review starts from your contracts and statements, not from a form.

General information as at 9 October 2026. Treatment depends on residence, entity, contracts, supply location and current law. This paper is not a filing instruction or an opinion on a particular creator. Contract-level conclusions and bank filing mechanics require individual review.
